Sexual Dimorphism in Phylum Cnidaria
Introduction to Sexual Dimorphism:
      Sexual dimorphism refers to the differences in size, color, structure, or appearance between male
and female members of the same species, beyond just their reproductive organs. In the Phylum Cnidaria,
sexual dimorphism is commonly observed in various species, particularly in terms of reproductive
features and body morphology.

Sexual Dimorphism in Cnidaria
      Members of Cnidaria exhibit sexual dimorphism mainly during their reproductive cycles. This
dimorphism is most evident in species that have distinct male and female forms, or those where males
and females differ in size, shape, or function.

1. Dimorphism in Size:
       In many cnidarians, females are typically larger than males. This size difference is often observed
in species where females need to accommodate a large number of eggs. For example, in certain species
of jellyfish, such as Aurelia aurita, the female is significantly larger than the male. The larger body size
allows the female to store and produce a greater quantity of eggs.

2. Dimorphism in Morphology:
     Sexual dimorphism can also manifest in differences in morphology. In some species, males and
females may have differently shaped reproductive organs or distinct external features that assist in
reproduction. For example, in the coral species Acropora, males and females have distinct gonads (testes
and ovaries), with males often having smaller gonads compared to the larger, more developed ovaries of
females.

3. Dimorphism in Behavioral Traits:
      Some cnidarians also show sexual dimorphism in their behaviors, particularly during the
reproductive phase. Males may exhibit specific mating behaviors or perform rituals to attract females.
For instance, in certain species of hydroids, males will release sperm into the water, while females
passively release eggs, which are then fertilized externally.

Example: Sexual Dimorphism in Aurelia aurita (Moon Jellyfish)
       In Aurelia aurita, a commonly studied jellyfish species, sexual dimorphism is clear. The females
are typically larger and have a broader bell compared to the males. The males release sperm into the
water during the reproductive season, while females are responsible for producing and carrying eggs
until they mature. This size difference allows for the efficient fertilization and development of offspring.

Conclusion
     Sexual dimorphism in Cnidaria plays a significant role in reproductive success. Differences in size,
morphology, and behavior enhance the reproductive strategies of males and females, ensuring effective
mating and offspring production in this diverse group of animals.

Chordates.
Phylum chordata is the largest group of Deuterostomes. Blastopore develop into
Anus during embryonic development. Most of the present day Chordates are
familiar vertebrates like fishes, amphibians,reptiles,birds and mammals besides
marine mammals like Dolphins and Whales. Nearly 49,000 species of chordates are
recorded.
Distribution: Chordates are found in the marine waters, fresh water and in the air.
Birds and mammals could go and live in the cold climate because they have a
constant body temperature (stenothermic).
Important fundamental Chordate Characters:

(1) Notochord

(2) Dorsal tubular nerve cord

(3) Pharyngeal gill slits

(4) Post anal tail
Notochord or chorda dorsalis:
     It develops from the Endodermal layer of embryonic archenteron.
     It consists of large vacuolated notochord cells containing gelatinous matrix.
     It is surrounded by outer fibrous sheath and inner elastic sheath.
     Notochord is present as an elongated rod-like, flexible structure running all
      along the length of the animal.

   It is situated immediately below the nerve cord and just above the alimentary
     canal.
   The notochord serves as a supporting internal skeleton which differs with the
     nerve cord both in its structure and function.
   In Protochordates it is present even in adults but in higher vertebrates it is
     replaced by vertebral column. Presence of notochord is a fundamental
     chordate character.
Dorsal Nerve cord:
   Dorsal nerve cord represents the central nervous system of the chordates.
   The nerve cord is a hollow tubular structure which is parallel to the
     notochord and present above it.
   The hollow cavity of the cord is called as Neurocoel which is derived from
     the ectodermal neural plate of the embryo. The main function of the nerve
     cord is to maintain the integration and co ordination of activities of an
     animal.
   In chordates (Vertebrates) the anterior part of the nerve cord enlarges into a
     vesicle which forms the brain and the posterior part becomes the spinal cord
     in the adult, enclosed within the Vertebral column.
Pharyngeal gill slits:
      In all chordates during their developmental stages, just behind the mouth
         in the pharyngeal wall, series of lateral gill slits or gill clefts are formed
         and they are termed or named as pharyngeal, branchial and visceral clefts
         or pouches.
      These structures help in passing out of water from pharynx over the
         external gills to outside. The water current also helps in filter feeding of
         the by filtering food particles present in water.
      In protochordates and in all fishes the gill slits are persistent or remain
         throughout the life carrying aquatic or gill respiration. In higher
         vertebrates they disappear during developmental stages and modified to
         acquire pulmonary respiration.
      During early embryonic life of all chordates the above said three
         characters are present. These characters are rarely persist in the adult
         chordates (e.g., Branchiostoma) and either modified or lost in the adult
         stage.
      In many chordates the notochord disappear but the nerve cord and the
         pharyngeal clefts remain in the adult.

Topic: Ecdysis or Molting

1. What is ecdysis? (1 mark)

2. Why it is required in insects? (1 mark)

3. Write four steps involved in the process of Ecdysis. (3 marks)

4. Make a handwritten diagram showing the steps involved in the process of Ecdysis in

an insect. Ensure that your diagram is labeled clearly. (5 marks)

1. What is ecdysis?

Ecdysis, or molting, is a biological process wherein arthropods, including insects, shed their old
exoskeleton to allow growth or morphological changes. The exoskeleton is a rigid, non-living
structure made of chitin and proteins, providing protection, support, and a barrier against water
loss. However, this rigidity prevents the organism from increasing in size as it grows. Ecdysis is
triggered by hormonal changes, particularly the release of ecdysone, which initiates the process.

The process involves enzymatic digestion of the inner layers of the old exoskeleton and the
synthesis of a new, larger cuticle underneath. After shedding the old exoskeleton, the new cuticle
is initially soft and pliable, allowing the organism to expand by absorbing air or water before it
hardens. Ecdysis is a critical and vulnerable period for arthropods, as they lack the protection of
a hardened exoskeleton during this time.

2. Why is it required in insects?

Ecdysis is vital for insects because their exoskeleton is inflexible and does not grow with the
organism. As the insect grows, the exoskeleton becomes restrictive, preventing further
development. To accommodate growth, the old exoskeleton must be shed and replaced with a
larger one. This process is especially important during the juvenile stages of development, such
as in nymphs and larvae.

In addition to facilitating growth, ecdysis is essential for insects undergoing metamorphosis. For
instance, in holometabolous insects, such as butterflies, the transition from larva to pupa and
pupa to adult involves significant structural changes, all requiring ecdysis. Moreover, shedding
the exoskeleton allows the insect to remove any accumulated debris, pathogens, or parasites that
may have adhered to it. Without ecdysis, insects would be unable to grow, reproduce, or survive
long-term.

                                                             By M.Kashif(03064963933)

3. Write four steps involved in the process of ecdysis.

   1. Apolysis: The process begins with the separation of the old exoskeleton from the
      epidermis beneath it. This is initiated by the secretion of ecdysone, which triggers the
      epidermal cells to produce molting fluid. The molting fluid contains enzymes that digest
      the inner layers of the old exoskeleton, starting the degradation process.
   2. Secretion of the New Cuticle: As the molting fluid breaks down the old exoskeleton, the
      epidermis starts synthesizing a new cuticle beneath the old one. This cuticle is soft and
      contains layers of proteins and chitin, which will harden and form the new exoskeleton.
   3. Shedding of the Old Exoskeleton: The insect inflates its body by swallowing air or
      water, creating pressure that causes the old exoskeleton to crack along pre-determined
      lines called ecdysial sutures. The insect then wriggles out of the old exoskeleton,
      exposing the new, soft cuticle underneath.
   4. Hardening and Darkening of the New Exoskeleton: After the old exoskeleton is shed,
      the new cuticle undergoes a process called sclerotization. This involves the cross-linking
      of proteins, which hardens and strengthens the exoskeleton. Pigments are also deposited,
      giving the exoskeleton its characteristic color. This step ensures the insect’s structural
      integrity and protection.

Question 1: Explain briefly sexual dimorphism in members of Phylum Cnidaria
with an example. (3 Marks)

Answer:
Sexual dimorphism refers to the distinct differences in appearance, structure, or reproductive
roles between male and female individuals of the same species. In Phylum Cnidaria, sexual
dimorphism is generally less pronounced than in higher animals but is still present in some
species—especially during the medusa stage, where separate male and female individuals exist.

Cnidarians typically reproduce both asexually (in the polyp stage) and sexually (in the medusa
stage). In species that display sexual dimorphism, male medusae produce sperm, and female
medusae produce eggs, which are usually released into the water column for external
fertilization.

Example – Aurelia aurita (Moon Jellyfish):
In Aurelia aurita, a common scyphozoan jellyfish, the male medusa releases sperm into the
water, which enters the female medusa’s oral arms where internal fertilization occurs. Female
medusae often have distinguishable gonads that can be observed through their transparent bell.
This reproductive separation between sexes is an example of sexual dimorphism in Cnidarians.

Some hydrozoans also exhibit dioecy, where male and female gametes are produced by separate
individuals, though their external morphology may be similar.

what is trapping
Animal trapping, or simply trapping or gin, is the use of a device to remotely catch an animal.
Animals may be trapped for a variety of purposes, including food, the fur trade, hunting, pest
control, and wildlife management.

Define Flukes?
The approximately eight thousand species of parasitic flatworms in the class Trematoda (Gr.
trematodes, perforated form) are collectively called flukes, which describes their wide, flat
shape. Almost all adult flukes are parasites of vertebrates, whereas immature stages may be
found in vertebrates or invertebrates, or encysted on plants.

Define Ocelli:
Ocelli are concerned in some way with flight, and insects which are good at flying tend to have
well developed ocelli. Ocelli consist of 500 to1,000 receptor cells beneath a single cuticular lens.
Ocelli are sensitive to changes in light intensity. Ocelli are simple photoreceptors. They consist
of a single lens and several sensory cells.

Acoelomate Examples

Examples of acoelomates are found in the kingdom Animalia and the phylum Platyhelminthes.
Commonly known as flatworms, Others are parasitic and often pathogenic organisms that live
within other animal organisms. Examples of flatworms include planarians, flukes, and
tapeworms. Ribbon worms of the phylum Nemertea have historically been considered to be
acoelomates. However, these mainly free-living worms have a specialized cavity called a
rhynchocoel that some consider to be a true coelom.

Determinate cleavage:
Cleavage is a process of rapid mitotic cell divisions of the zygote to form number of cells for
building up the offspring’s body.It results in developmental fate of cells being set early in
embryo development. Cell division in a fertilized or unfertilized egg resulting in daughter cells
that are no longer able to produce a complete embryo by themselves.

Write down the body form of sponges?
Zoologist have described three sponge body forms:
1. Asconoid
2. Syconoid
3. Leuconoid
1=The simplest and least common sponge body form is the ascon. Simplest type of canal system
found in asconoid sponges. Ascon sponges are vaselike. Ostia are the outer openings of
porocytes and lead directly to a chamber called the spongocoal
2=In the sycon body form, the sponge wall appears folded.Water enters a sycon sponge through
openings called dermal pores.
3=Leucon sponges have an extensively branched canal system. Water enters the sponge through
ostia and moves through branched incurrents canals, which lead to Choanocyte-lined chambers.

Write characteristics of class cestoda:
    Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes);
    they are ribbonlike worms as adults, known as tapeworms.
    Their bodies consist of many similar units, known as proglottids.
    Species of the other subclass, Cestodaria, are mainly fish parasites.
    Cestodes have no gut or mouth and absorb nutrients from the host's alimentary tract by
     their tegument, through which gas exchange also takes place.
    The tegument also protects the parasite from the host's digestive enzymes and allows it to
     transfer molecules back to the host.
    Reproduction: Cestodes are exclusively hermaphrodites, cross-fertilization is the norm.
     During copulation, the cirri of one individual connect with those of the other through the
     genital pore and then spermatozoa are exchanged.

Alarm Pheromones:
Alarm pheromones are defined as chemical substances, produced and released by an organism,
that warn or alertanother of the same species of impending danger. Its provide the Alarm signals
visual or auditory.

Describe the life cycle of insect?
Some insects (like butterflies, but also beetles, flies, and bees) develop by complete
metamorphosis with 4 life stages: egg, larva, pupa, and adult.

Describe the Mating behavior of Insects?
    Most insects have complex mating behaviors for locating and recognizing a potential
     mate, for positioning a mate for copulation, or for pacifying an aggressive mate.
    Mating behavior may involve pheromones (moths, order Lepidoptera), visual signals
     (fireflies, order Coleoptera), and auditory signals (cicadas, order Homoptera; and
     grasshoppers, crickets, and katydids, order Orthoptera)
    Once other stimuli have brought the male and female together, tactile stimuli from the
     antennae and other appendages help position the insects for mating.
    Mating behavior starts by locating mates. Male and female have different strategies
     toward copulation and reproduction.
    After locating mates is courtship; one male and female have encountered each other, they
     may proceed directly to copulation or may first engage in various rituals, collectively
     known as courtship.
    The final ritual is copulation.

Importance of Soil Dwelling Insects

    Weed Killers: So many insects feed upon unwanted weeds just the same manner they do
     with the cultivated crops.
    Scavengers: Insects which feed on dead and decaying matter of plants and animals are
     called as scavengers.
    Aeration and turnover of the soil: As decomposers, insects help create top soil, the
     nutrientrich layer of soil that helps plants grow.
    Promotion of decay process: In many ecosystems millipedes (Diplopoda) have special
     importance as decomposers.
    Role in food chain: Food for other animals: Many insects live on grass and plants for
     food. food insects but in-turn they become prey to many birds, amphibians, fishes,
     lizards, and other animals.

Describe the ventilating process in Insects?
   Most insects have ventilating mechanisms that move air into and out of the tracheal system.

    Insects do not breathe through their mouths as we do.

    The do not have lungs and their blood, which is a watery, yellowish liquid, does not carry
     oxygen and carbon dioxide around their bodies.
